headline: Nyatt Point after dark: stripers on bunker chunks, fluke holding steady off Prudence
subhead: The herring are long gone from Buckeye Brook, the bay's pushing warm, and the bass have gone nocturnal while fluke and scup carry the daylight hours.
body_markdown:
I was down at the Conimicut town dock Tuesday night listening to two guys argue about whether it was worth running lines out past ten o'clock, and one of them said something that stuck with me: "Buckeye's been dry since May, bud, this ain't that fish no more." He's right. That herring run that gets everybody's blood up every spring — the one that pulls bass up into the Warren and Barrington rivers chasing river herring stacked thick enough to walk on — that's done and gone for the season. What's left now is a different animal. Bigger, warier, and mostly a creature of the dark.

The bay's been running warm, pushing into the low-to-mid 70s on the surface, same story that's got bass locked into a low-light pattern from here down through the Sound and the Jersey beaches. During the day the fish just aren't interested in banging around in bright water — too much effort for too little payoff. So they're doing what smart striped bass do in July: sliding into deeper water and structure through the afternoon, then coming up to feed hard in that hour before dark and again well after the lights come on.

That's exactly what's happening under the Nyatt Point bridge and around the pilings at the old Rocky Point pier. Guys are soaking chunk bunker on fishfinder rigs in 15 to 20 feet, right on the edge of the light line where the current sweeps bait past the structure on the last two hours of the ebb. I had a 29-incher there myself Thursday night on a chunk, and heard of a couple fish pushing 34, 35 inches taken the same window on live eels swung off the current seam below the bridge. If you're going to fish it, fish it slow and quiet — no spotlights on the water, no slamming hatches. These bay bass have seen enough boat traffic to get cagey.

Daytime, it's fluke and scup carrying the weight, and that bite's been the more dependable one all week. Fluke are holding on the channel edges off Prudence Island and along the drop outside Greenwich Bay, working best on the last stretch of the outgoing into the first half hour of the flood when the current's still got some push to it. Four-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow along bottom in 20 to 28 feet — that combo's been putting keeper-class fluke in the box, nothing giant but steady, a fish or two on most drifts if you're patient about covering ground.

Scup are stacked on the rocky ledges the way they always are this time of year — Conimicut Point out to the can, the rock piles off Nyatt, and the ledge work up toward Rocky Point. Incoming tide is the move, small hooks, sandworms or clam bait, light enough tackle that you can feel every pluck. Nothing fancy about it, just steady meat-and-potatoes fishing that fills a cooler if you've got the patience to sit on the anchor.

Here's the one I want to flag: we said last week the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly what's happening in Greenwich Bay and up around Bullocks Point. Squid have been running into the bay in decent numbers, which is a good sign for bait availability across the board, and the weakfish have been sliding up on those calm dusk tides to work the edges where the squid concentrate. Small swim shads and soft plastic shrimp imitations worked slow just off bottom at last light have been drawing strikes — nothing huge, mostly schoolies in the 16 to 20 inch range, but a legit bite where there wasn't much of one two weeks ago.

Sea bass are still there for anybody willing to make the run out toward Dutch Island and the humps off the west side of Prudence — squid strips and clam on bottom rigs in 25 to 35 feet, best on the last of the ebb when the current settles enough to hold bottom without dragging your sinker halfway to Newport. Sizes have been decent, a few fish pushing four and five pounds mixed in with the usual dinner-plate class.

Bluefish have been more of a rumor than a pattern in the bay proper this week — a few scattered blitzes on peanut bunker up around Conimicut and off Nayatt, but nothing sustained. If the bunker schools that have been working the beaches outside the bay decide to push in further, that could change fast, and it's worth keeping an eye on the surface for diving terns.

We're heading into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the current through the bridges and the ledge spots for a few days. That's not a bad thing — it widens the productive window on the fluke drifts and takes some of the urgency out of hitting peak tide exactly right on the scup grounds. What I'd do this week: fish the bridges and points after dark for bass on chunk and eel, hit Prudence and outside Greenwich Bay midday for fluke on the moving water, and keep a rod rigged light for weakfish if you're out at dusk with calm conditions. If the squid keep pushing into the bay the way they have been, that weakfish bite has room to build further before the month's out.
